rv.q: In fact, director Thom Southerland's bare-boards adaptation, using Szpilman's own compositions and deploying an ensemble of actor-musicians around a sombrely black baby grand piano, is a qualified success.
It’s a project lovingly done, and with great potential, but it needs turbocharging, possibly with more experienced actors.
The Pianist only intermittently achieves its full emotional potential, possibly due to a central character who keeps himself, and us, slightly at arms length throughout.

It's a piece that could hardly not be affecting, with its sepia-tinted depiction of old world Jewry and bohemianism that are accompanied by Szpilman's own compositions, but it's not as confronting as the subject matter deserves.
It is a haunting piece of theatre that stays with you long after you leave the auditorium – and one that makes the silence after the final note feel just as powerful as the music itself.
That is why this production feels so necessary right now.
This is still a beautiful piece of theatre, that puts the music in the centre of it all, right where it should be.
He puts in a stunning performance that could shake even the most hardened to the core.
The story of the Jewish ‘Polish Gershwin’ is blessed to have an actor as talented as Krikler at its centre.

cn.t: Critics praise this emotionally powerful musical adaptation of Szpilman's WWII memoir, with many calling it heartbreaking and extraordinary. The intimate staging and use of music resonate strongly, though reception ranges from moved to merely solid.
